summary: A report by J. Pickens at UCSB evaluating ARPANET services from January through March 1972, from a group set up to try out network resources. It reports many unexpected problems, mainly differing software and poor documentation, and gives criteria for ease of use plus suggestions for improvement. It follows on from RFC 302.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 369 reports on UCSB students who tried ARPANET services as new users during January through March 1972. They found that different sites worked in different ways, documentation was hard to find, and reliable access was limited.

questions: what problems did early arpanet users face
what is friendliness in network services
subtitle: A UCSB group evaluates ARPANET services from the viewpoint of new users.

tldr.problem: New users had trouble finding, reaching, and using ARPANET resources, but site surveys had mostly measured hardware and host software rather than user experience.
tldr.mechanism: A UCSB graduate student group explored network sites for nine weeks, completed a questionnaire, and rated sites for reliability, response, and friendliness.
tldr.outcome: The report identifies software differences and inadequate documentation as major problems and proposes shorter user guides, better network information, and a consulting center.

today: The unit metadata lists RFC 369's status as Unknown and no RFC as obsoleting or updating it. It is a report on the ARPANET user experience during January through March 1972 and builds on RFC 302.

sections.title: The Group's Approach
sections.content:
RFC 302 describes the UCSB group organized to investigate ARPANET resources. The students had experience with programming languages and time-sharing systems, but none had experience using ARPANET. After two weeks of presentations, they explored network sites and shared procedures during their seminar.

The group aimed to learn how to use network resources and evaluate them fairly, including UCSB's own site. The report notes that interest declined as the quarter continued, in part because of site reliability, the small number of active nodes, and hard-to-find documentation.
sections.plainLanguage: The students had to learn the network from scratch. They tried available services, shared what they learned, and recorded the difficulties they encountered.

sections.title: Survey Results
sections.content:
The main period of activity was January through March 1972. The group focused on UCSB, BBN-TENEX, MIT-MULTICS, and SRI-ARC, with smaller investigations of other sites. Activities included games, text and file work, messaging, and online compilation.

Twelve students answered a questionnaire after nine weeks of experience. On average, respondents reported trouble-free operation 35% of the time and estimated a mean time between failures of one hour. The report warns that the questions did not distinguish failures at a remote node from failures in the user's local NCP.
sections.plainLanguage: The survey found that students had trouble-free use only about a third of the time. The authors caution that the questionnaire could not always show which part of the connection caused a problem.

sections.title: Friendliness and Common Problems
sections.content:
The report defines “friendliness” through clear and complete documentation, easy system use, accessible help, concise messages, reasonable reliability and response time, and useful error messages. It says the most annoying difficulty was finding adequate documentation.

Students also found that similar tasks required different commands at different sites. Editors, file names, compilation procedures, and ways to return to a system's top level varied. The report describes this software heterogeneity as a stumbling block and also notes uneven help from other researchers and difficulty finding who was responsible for a resource.
sections.plainLanguage: A service is easier to use when its instructions are clear, help is available, and errors explain what happened. The students found that each site often handled the same task differently.

sections.title: Suggested Improvements
sections.content:
The group suggests working groups for tasks that need several network resources and more use of the services already available. It recommends a short self-contained user manual for each site and network-wide function, covering login, file editing, compilation, Telnet access, programs, and how to get help.

Other suggestions include high-level calls to each NCP, regular concise network news, stronger use of interpersonal communication tools, and a consulting center, perhaps at the NIC, to match users with resources. The report says students had written programs for automatic login, file transfer, and interprocess communication.
sections.plainLanguage: The students recommend short practical guides, easier ways for programs to use each NCP, and a place to help users find network resources. They also encourage people to use the network's communication services more often.

references.text: RFC 302, "Exercising the ARPANET", describing the UCSB group.
